raw_response:
I have farmed these 6 mu in Quzhou County for more than thirty years. I only went to primary school, but I know this land and this weather. I do not chase fancy crops or gamble with prices. Every household around me grows winter wheat followed by summer maize, and that is what I will do this year too. It is the only rotation that gives me two harvests in twelve months and lets me sell to the grain trader at the village gate without worry. My wheat is already in the ground from last October; now I must topdress it, irrigate three times through the spring drought, and spray for weeds, insects, and maybe a little rust. I always rotary-till before wheat sowing because it breaks the stubble and warms the soil. After I cut the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid maize with no-tillage direct seeding—there is no time to plough, and the village machinery cooperative charges less for no-till anyway. I will give the maize two good irrigations and three rounds of spray. I use less fertilizer on maize than on wheat because the wheat stubble and roots left in the soil still feed the next crop. I do not grow cotton or melons; their prices jump around, and my back is not getting any younger at fifty-five. Wheat and maize may not make me rich, but they fill the grain bags and pay for my grandson’s school fees. That is enough for me.
